strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored question: the empirical geometric relationship between initial noise, generated samples, and DDIM-inverted latents, which is directly relevant to the many downstream inversion-based editing methods.

The experimental protocol is fairly thorough for an empirical/analysis paper: three different model families (pixel-space DDPM on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and an LDM on CelebA), multiple metrics (Pearson correlation, angles, L2 distances, KNN coverage, CKA/SSIM/SVCCA/DINO alignment), and training-time dynamics via checkpoints.

The finding that latents lie geometrically between the noise and the sample along (close to) the generation trajectory, and that this relationship stabilizes very early in training, is an interesting and reasonably well-supported empirical observation that ties together several previously scattered qualitative observations (e.g., Renoise, Parmar et al., Kadkhodaie et al.) into a more systematic study.

The paper provides a reasonably careful ablation on the number of diffusion steps T (Appendix A.2), showing how the noise-latent-image geometry evolves with T, which strengthens the robustness of the core geometric claim.

The noise-to-sample nearest-neighbor assignment experiment and its evolution across training is a clean and interpretable way to demonstrate that the mapping structure emerges early, complementing the alignment-metric results in Figure 7.
weaknesses: The contribution is purely observational/empirical with no proposed method, theoretical explanation, or actionable technique to fix the identified DDIM inversion inaccuracy; the practical implications for the many downstream editing/inversion methods referenced in related work are not directly tested (e.g., no editing task, no reconstruction quality benchmark tied to the geometric findings).

The datasets and models used are quite small-scale and dated for a 2024+ submission (CIFAR-10 32x32, ImageNet 64x64, CelebA via a small LDM) — no experiments with modern large-scale text-to-image diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion, SDXL) where inversion techniques are actually most heavily used in practice, which limits the generalizability and significance of the claims to the settings where inversion matters most (text-to-image editing).

The explanation for why generated-to-noise reverse assignment fails at high T (attraction to low-variance/plain images) is presented mostly through a handful of qualitative examples (Appendix A.1) rather than a rigorous quantitative analysis of why this occurs or how it relates to the model's implicit bias or η/guidance settings.

Some claims are stated more strongly than the evidence supports, e.g., 'the relation between images and noises is defined by simple L2 distance at the early stage of training' is based on nearest-neighbor accuracy under a specific number of samples (N=1000) and specific T values, and it is unclear how this scales with larger sample pools or higher-dimensional/more complex datasets.

The related work on optimal transport (Khrulkov & Oseledets) and consistency (Kadkhodaie et al., Zhang et al.) is closely related in spirit and the paper's incremental contribution relative to these existing findings (that generation is close to an optimal-transport-like nearest-noise mapping, and that this converges early) is not always clearly differentiated — the paper reads at several points as confirming/extending known results rather than establishing fundamentally new phenomena.

No classifier-free guidance or conditional/text-to-image settings are studied, despite the introduction and background explicitly flagging CFG as a major source of DDIM inversion error, which is a substantial gap given the motivation of the paper.

The presentation of quantitative results (e.g., Table 1, Table 2) would benefit from clearer statistical significance testing and from including a wider range of T and guidance scales in the main text rather than relegated appendices, given how central these design choices are to the paper's core claims.

The paper lacks a clear discussion of practical recommendations or design implications for practitioners of inversion-based editing methods, limiting its downstream significance despite highlighting a real problem.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and relevant question: characterizing the geometric relationship between initial Gaussian noise, generated samples, and DDIM-inverted latents.
Experiments span three different model types/datasets (pixel-space DDPM on CIFAR-10, DDPM on ImageNet, LDM on CelebA), providing some diversity of settings.
The training-dynamics experiments (Figures 4-7) showing that the noise-sample mapping and low-frequency content stabilize early in training are a mildly interesting empirical observation.
Reasonably thorough set of diagnostic tools (correlation coefficients, angle/triangle visualizations, KNN coverage, image-alignment metrics such as CKA/SSIM/SVCCA/DINO).
Appendix provides some robustness checks across different numbers of diffusion steps T.
weaknesses: The core findings largely restate or empirically re-confirm observations already reported in the cited literature (e.g., Garibi et al. 2024; Parmar et al. 2023; Hong et al. 2024 on non-Gaussian DDIM latents; Khrulkov & Oseledets 2022 and Zhang et al. 2024 on noise-to-image mapping and optimal transport), so the incremental novelty of the contribution is limited.

The paper is purely observational/descriptive: it identifies phenomena but proposes no new method, correction, theoretical explanation, or actionable improvement to inversion techniques or editing pipelines, limiting its significance and practical impact.

No theoretical grounding is offered for the central empirical claims (e.g., why latents fall 'between' noise and image, why nearest-neighbor noise assignment works); given known concentration-of-measure effects in high dimensions, some of the reported phenomena (e.g., near-unique nearest-noise assignment) could plausibly be explained by simpler statistical arguments that are not explored or ruled out.

Experiments are restricted to small, low-resolution, unconditional models (32×32 CIFAR-10, 64×64 ImageNet, CelebA via LDM); no experiments on modern large-scale/text-to-image diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) despite the motivation being heavily framed around editing methods that are used almost exclusively with such models today, which weakens the relevance and generalizability of the conclusions.

Averaging angles/distances across thousands of samples into a single representative triangle (Figure 2) is methodologically questionable, since it may not represent the geometry of any individual sample and could mask high variance in per-sample relationships; per-sample distributions or variance of these angles are not reported.

The explanation for reverse-assignment failure (low-variance images attracting most noises) is a fairly mundane nearest-neighbor collapse phenomenon and is not analyzed rigorously (e.g., no comparison to a null model or theoretical rate).
Fine-tuning experiments for training dynamics use only two small models (CIFAR-10, ImageNet) with three seeds each, limiting the breadth and statistical confidence of the training-time conclusions.
Some tables have missing or incomplete entries (e.g., Table 1 does not report noise correlation for CelebA/LDM), and the paper does not discuss whether these gaps affect interpretation.

The paper does not connect its findings back to improving existing inversion techniques (e.g., Null-text inversion, ReNoise) or to any downstream editing task, leaving the significance of the results largely academic without demonstrated utility for the community.

strengths: Provides a clear, systematic geometric characterization of the relationship between initial noise, generated samples, and DDIM-inverted latents (triangle angle/distance analysis), which nicely operationalizes and quantifies a phenomenon that was previously only qualitatively noted in prior work.
Experiments span three different model types/datasets (pixel-space DDPM on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and LDM on CelebA), lending some generality to the observations.

The training-dynamics analysis (Figures 4-7) is the most novel and interesting contribution: showing that the noise-latent-sample geometric relationship and the noise-to-sample mapping are established very early in training and remain essentially fixed afterward, which has practical implications for understanding what training time is 'used for'.
Good use of multiple complementary metrics (Pearson correlation, angles, L2 distances, CKA/DINO/SSIM/SVCCA) to substantiate claims from different angles.
Reasonably transparent about limitations of DDIM inversion (linearization approximation) and ties observations back to the theoretical assumption in Eq. 4, giving a plausible mechanistic explanation.
Appendix experiments on varying T strengthen the robustness of the main claims and show the effect is not merely an artifact of a specific step count.
weaknesses: The paper is purely diagnostic/observational: it identifies known issues (non-Gaussianity of inverted latents, imperfect DDIM inversion) that have already been pointed out by cited works (Garibi et al. 2024; Parmar et al. 2023; Hong et al. 2024), and does not propose any new method, fix, or actionable technique to mitigate the problem.

The noise-to-sample mapping accuracy findings largely corroborate and extend prior work (Kadkhodaie et al. 2023/2024; Zhang et al. 2024; Khrulkov & Oseledets 2022) rather than introducing a substantially new phenomenon, limiting the incremental novelty.

All experiments use small-scale, low-resolution unconditional models (32x32 CIFAR-10, 64x64 ImageNet, and a modest LDM on CelebA); it's unclear whether the conclusions transfer to the large-scale, text-conditioned, classifier-free-guidance diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) that are the primary target of the inversion techniques discussed in the related work and motivation.

No downstream validation: despite motivating the work via editing/inpainting applications, the paper never tests how these geometric findings actually impact real editing quality or inversion-based tasks, leaving the practical significance somewhat speculative.

The explanation for reverse-assignment failures (x^T -> x^0) — that a few low-variance images attract most noises — is somewhat superficial and not analyzed rigorously (e.g., no discussion of why this happens theoretically or how it interacts with the score function's properties).

Some claims (e.g., 'defining the relation at early training') are demonstrated on only two models (CIFAR-10 and ImageNet DDPMs) without the LDM, reducing generality of the training-dynamics conclusions.

Presentation is at times dense and hard to follow (e.g., Figure 2/3 captions, notation-heavy Appendix tables), and some figures (e.g., Figure 1) rely on informal visual inspection rather than quantitative support.
Limited statistical rigor around the correlation analysis in Table 1 (e.g., no correction for multiple comparisons, no discussion of sample size sufficiency for top-10 correlations).

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical analysis spanning six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space ADMs at multiple resolutions, LDM, DiT, DeepFloyd IF) and datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA-HQ, LAION-A), lending credibility and generality to the observed phenomena.

The paper builds a coherent causal narrative across four well-motivated research questions: it first confirms known deviations of DDIM latents from Gaussian noise, then localizes this deviation geometrically and statistically to smooth/plain image regions, then traces the root cause to higher approximation error in the first few inversion steps, and finally demonstrates practical downstream consequences (interpolation quality collapse, reduced editing diversity, noise-to-image mapping asymmetry).
The geometric triangle analysis (Sec 3.3) and trajectory-distance analysis (Fig. 3) are a creative and informative way to visualize where latents sit relative to noise and image manifolds.

The causal claim is validated via an intervention experiment (replacing the first ~6-10% of inversion steps with ground-truth backward-diffusion predictions), which meaningfully reduces latent correlation, KL divergence to Gaussian, and downstream artifacts, strengthening the mechanistic explanation beyond mere correlation.

Extensive and well-organized supplementary material, including ablations over number of diffusion steps T, training-time dynamics of noise-image-latent relations, and detailed methodology descriptions, supports reproducibility and robustness of the claims.

Practical consequences are quantified with multiple relevant metrics (FID, Precision/Recall, DreamSim, LPIPS, SSIM, DINO, CLIP text alignment), providing convincing evidence that the identified latent-space limitations translate into real degradations in interpolation and editing tasks.
weaknesses: The paper is primarily an analysis/explanatory study rather than proposing a new, practically deployable method; the mitigation strategy in Sec. 5 relies on oracle access to ground-truth backward-diffusion noise predictions, which is not available for real (non-generated) images used in typical editing workflows, limiting practical applicability.

Central qualitative findings (that DDIM latents deviate from Gaussian noise due to approximation error) were already noted by prior work (Parmar et al., Garibi et al., Wallace et al.); the paper's novelty rests mainly on further mechanistic dissection (plain vs. non-plain regions, early-step localization) rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon or method, which may be seen as incremental for a top-tier venue.

All experiments disable classifier-free guidance (w=1) to isolate approximation error, but CFG is used in essentially all practical text-to-image editing/inversion pipelines; this significantly limits the ecological validity of the findings for the very editing applications the paper motivates itself with (e.g., Null-text inversion, prompt-to-prompt), and no experiments verify whether the same plain-region effect and its early-step origin persist under CFG.

No comparison against existing improved inversion techniques (Null-text Inversion, EDICT, ReNoise, exact DPM-solver inversion, etc.) to check whether these methods already mitigate (or fail to mitigate) the identified plain-region/early-step divergence, which would have made the paper's practical relevance much stronger.

The angle-based triangle methodology (Appendix B) for characterizing noise-sample-latent geometry, while creative, is not rigorously justified as meaningful for capturing manifold structure beyond a coarse heuristic, and its practical implications for downstream use are not explored.

The paper does not offer a concrete, generalizable fix that practitioners could adopt in real-world use cases beyond the illustrative ground-truth-substitution ablation, leaving the actionable takeaway somewhat limited despite the thorough diagnosis.

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical analysis spanning six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space ADMs at multiple resolutions, latent-space LDM and DiT, and conditional Deepfloyd IF), which adds some robustness to the observed trends.

The paper isolates a specific, testable explanation for previously known DDIM-inversion/Gaussian-noise mismatch: higher approximation error in plain/smooth image regions, concentrated in the earliest inversion steps. This is a more fine-grained diagnosis than prior work that simply notes the mismatch exists.

Reasonably thorough set of downstream consequence experiments (interpolation FID/precision/recall, conditional-editing diversity/text-alignment, noise-to-image/latent-to-image nearest-neighbor mapping) that consistently support the central narrative.

The final experiment showing that substituting ground-truth predictions for only the first ~6-10% of inversion steps sharply reduces pixel correlation and reconstruction/KL divergence is a nice, low-cost ablation that strengthens the causal claim.
Supplementary material is unusually extensive (training-dynamics experiments, angle-triangle methodology, mapping asymmetry analysis), showing effort toward reproducibility and robustness checks.
weaknesses: Core finding that DDIM-inverted latents deviate from Gaussian noise and hurt editability is already established by cited prior work (Parmar et al., Garibi et al., Hong et al., Wallace et al.); the paper's added value is mainly a more detailed localization (plain regions, early steps) rather than a fundamentally new insight, which is a fairly incremental contribution for a top-tier venue.

The paper is purely diagnostic/analytical with no proposed method or fix for practitioners; the one mitigation shown (replacing early inversion steps with ground-truth model outputs) requires access to the actual forward/backward diffusion trajectory, which is circular and only feasible for self-generated images, not for real-world images that are the primary use case of inversion-based editing. This substantially limits the practical significance of the 'solution' offered in Sec. 5.

Most experiments disable classifier-free guidance (w=1) to isolate inversion error, but CFG is precisely what practitioners use for meaningful prompt-driven editing; it is unclear how much the findings and their magnitude generalize to the CFG>1 regime where most real editing pipelines operate, and no experiments address this gap.

The geometric 'most probable triangle angle' analysis (Sec. 3.3, Appendix B) is methodologically ad hoc (binning discretized angles and maximizing a joint probability under an assumed independence-like combination) and its interpretive value beyond confirming the already-known correlation finding is unclear; it does not obviously add actionable insight.

No comparison to specialized inversion methods (Null-text Inversion, EDICT, ReNoise, Edit-Friendly DDPM inversion, etc.) to test whether the identified plain-region/early-step error also afflicts these already-published improvements, which would have made the analysis much more useful for the field by showing whether existing fixes already solve (or fail to solve) the diagnosed problem.

The interpolation/editing experiments are conducted mostly on unconditional or simplified conditional setups (ImageNet class names for DiT, single COCO captions for IF) rather than realistic, complex editing scenarios, limiting the ecological validity of the demonstrated 'consequences'.

Several quantitative claims (e.g., Table 5, Table 6) rely on a hand-tuned plain/non-plain threshold (τ=0.025) without sensitivity analysis, raising concerns about robustness of the plain-vs-non-plain distinction underlying the paper's central claim.

The overall contribution reads more like a workshop-level empirical study/negative-results report than a paper with a clear methodological advance, evaluation against baselines, or new technique, which weakens its case for a top-tier full-paper acceptance.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical analysis spanning six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space and latent-space, conditional and unconditional) across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA-HQ, and LAION-A, lending good generality to the findings.

The paper builds a coherent narrative: (1) demonstrates latent deviation from Gaussian noise via correlation statistics, (2) localizes this deviation geometrically (angle analysis, trajectory distance) and to plain image regions, (3) traces the root cause to approximation error in the first few DDIM inversion steps, and (4) shows concrete downstream consequences for interpolation, editing diversity, and text alignment.

The geometric triangle analysis (Table 3, Fig. 3) and the noise-to-image/latent-to-image nearest-neighbor mapping experiments (Sec 4.3) offer novel and intuitive perspectives not covered by prior work on DDIM inversion errors.

The proposed mitigation (replacing only the first ~6-10% of inversion steps with ground-truth model outputs) is a clean, well-supported ablation that directly validates the causal claim about early-step errors, and quantitatively improves correlation, diversity, and text alignment.

Extensive supplementary material (masking methodology, additional angle statistics across different T, training-dynamics experiments showing noise-image mapping is established early in training) strengthens reproducibility and robustness of claims.

The practical implications (reduced diversity/editability of DDIM-inverted latents) are relevant to a widely used class of methods (image editing, interpolation) and could inform future inversion algorithm design.
weaknesses: The paper is purely observational/analytical; the only proposed remedy (substituting ground-truth denoiser outputs for early inversion steps) requires access to the ground-truth backward diffusion trajectory, which is unavailable for real (non-generated) images—the primary use case for inversion-based editing—limiting the practical impact of the main mitigation.

All main experiments disable classifier-free guidance (w=1), yet CFG is standard in practical text-to-image editing/interpolation pipelines and is known (as the paper itself notes, citing Mokady et al.) to introduce additional, likely larger, inversion error; it is unclear how much the reported effects generalize to the CFG-enabled regime actually used in downstream applications.

Novelty relative to prior work (Parmar et al., Garibi et al., Hong et al.) that already established non-Gaussianity of DDIM latents is incremental; the paper mainly adds finer-grained characterization (plain vs. non-plain regions, early-step localization) rather than a fundamentally new insight or technique.

The paper does not compare against existing improved-inversion methods (Null-text inversion, EDICT, ReNoise, edit-friendly DDPM inversion, etc.) to show whether these already mitigate the identified plain-region/early-step divergence, which would better contextualize the significance of the findings relative to the state of the art.

The 'most probable angle' methodology (independent per-vertex histogram binning and joint probability maximization) is somewhat ad hoc and not rigorously justified statistically; confidence intervals or alternative geometric summaries are not provided.

Evaluation of editing/interpolation quality relies solely on automated metrics (FID, LPIPS, DreamSim, CLIP, DINO, SSIM); no human evaluation is included to confirm perceptual relevance of the observed diversity/quality differences.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical analysis spanning six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space ADMs at multiple resolutions, latent diffusion LDM, DiT, IF), covering both conditional and unconditional models.

The paper builds a clear, well-organized narrative through four research questions, each supported by multiple complementary experiments (correlation statistics, angle/triangle geometry, variance analysis, per-pixel error decomposition).

Identifies a plausible and interesting root cause for the divergence between Gaussian noise and DDIM-inverted latents: disproportionately large approximation errors in early inversion steps concentrated in smooth/plain image regions, which is a nontrivial and useful diagnostic finding for the community.

The proposed fix (replacing the first few inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, computationally cheap (faster than baseline), and is evaluated with quantitative downstream benefits in interpolation (FID/precision/recall) and editing (diversity/alignment metrics like LPIPS, DreamSim, CLIP-T).

Very extensive appendix with reproducibility details (masking methodology, pseudocode, compute resources), robustness checks (varying T up to 1000/4000 steps), training-time dynamics analysis, and failure-case discussion, which strengthens scientific rigor and honesty about limitations.
Good visualizations (correlation maps, PCA plots, triangle geometry, qualitative editing/interpolation comparisons) that make the abstract statistical claims tangible.
weaknesses: The proposed remedy (substituting early DDIM inversion steps with a plain forward-diffusion step) is a fairly simple and somewhat expected engineering trick; conceptually it is similar to prior works that already leverage stochastic renoising or forward-diffusion-based re-initialization in editing pipelines (e.g., SDEdit-like strategies), so the technical novelty of the solution itself is limited even though the diagnostic analysis is more original.

No direct quantitative comparison against existing improved-inversion methods (e.g., ReNoise, Edit Friendly DDPM inversion, Null-text inversion, exact DPM-solver inversion) that also target reducing inversion error/correlation; the paper only compares plain DDIM inversion vs. their forward-diffusion variant, making it hard to judge whether the proposed fix is competitive with (or subsumed by) the existing correction techniques cited in Section 2.

The explanation of "why" errors concentrate in plain regions during early steps is largely empirical/correlational; no theoretical derivation or mechanistic proof is given connecting score-function curvature/smoothness of network output to this error pattern, despite acknowledging related theoretical works (curvature blow-up, singularity arguments) without formally integrating them.

The choice of how many initial steps to replace with forward diffusion (e.g., 2-6%) appears to be tuned per-model somewhat empirically, and the trade-off curve between reconstruction fidelity and editability, while shown in appendix (failure cases at 10-20%), is not deeply analyzed as an automatic/adaptive selection method — the fixed percentage heuristic may not generalize well across models/tasks without manual tuning.

The LDM/CelebA-HQ results are noted as an exception to the general pattern (Appendix A), which is only briefly explained by dataset homogeneity; this limits the strength of the claimed generality of the core finding.

Reconstruction quality metrics (e.g., LPIPS/PSNR/SSIM between original and reconstructed images) for the proposed method versus standard DDIM inversion are not prominently reported in the main text, making it harder to assess exactly how much fidelity is sacrificed for the reported editability/diversity gains outside of qualitative figures and a brief appendix table.

The paper's contribution is purely analytical for a well-studied problem (DDIM inversion quality), and while thorough, the significance/impact for downstream real-world applications (e.g., large-scale text-to-image editing with SDXL/Stable Diffusion 3, or comparison to more modern non-DDIM inversion techniques) is not demonstrated on state-of-the-art contemporary models, limiting practical impact evidence.

strengths: The analysis is conducted across a genuinely broad set of six diffusion architectures (pixel-space and latent-space, conditional and unconditional), which supports the generality of the main empirical claim that DDIM-inversion latents show reduced diversity/correlation in smooth image regions.

The paper offers a plausible and reasonably well-supported causal account for the phenomenon: it links the observed spatial correlations to a measurable, larger noise-prediction approximation error for plain-region pixels concentrated in the earliest inversion steps (Fig. 4, Table 6), going beyond simply re-confirming prior observations of correlated DDIM latents (e.g., Parmar et al., Garibi et al.).

Downstream consequences are evaluated with a fairly diverse and appropriate set of metrics (FID/Precision/Recall for interpolation; LPIPS/DreamSim/SSIM/DINO/CLIP-T for editing diversity and prompt alignment), and the proposed fix is shown to consistently improve these metrics across two conditioned models.

The appendix is unusually thorough, including additional generalization checks (T=1000 in App. E), a training-dynamics study (App. M) showing the noise-image-latent relationship is set early in training, and honest failure-case/limitation discussion (App. A, N.1) showing where the fix degrades reconstruction.
weaknesses: The proposed 'fix' (replacing the first few DDIM inversion steps with forward diffusion noising) is conceptually very close to well-established noise-injection practices in the editing literature (e.g., SDEdit-style intermediate noising, edit-friendly DDPM inversion), so the technical novelty of the solution itself is limited despite being framed as a new contribution; the paper does not clearly differentiate its method from these related noise-injection strategies beyond applying it specifically to the earliest DDIM steps.

No quantitative comparison is provided against existing inversion-improvement baselines that target the same editability/reconstruction trade-off (e.g., Null-text Inversion, ReNoise, Edit-Friendly DDPM inversion, Schedule-Your-Edit); the only baseline is vanilla DDIM inversion, making it hard to judge whether the proposed fix is competitive with or superior to prior remedies rather than just better than an intentionally naive baseline.

Several core methodological choices are ad hoc and under-justified: the plain/non-plain pixel mask relies on a fixed heuristic threshold (τ=0.025) on neighbor differences with no sensitivity analysis, and the 'most probable triangle' angle analysis (Section 3.2, Appendix F) is a non-standard construct whose interpretive value and robustness to binning/sample size are not rigorously established.

The method has an explicitly acknowledged failure mode on the LDM/CelebA-HQ model (Appendix A) that is dismissed with a post-hoc, untested explanation (uniform backgrounds/limited concept diversity), weakening the claim of general applicability across latent diffusion models.

The fix inherently trades off reconstruction fidelity against editability/diversity (Appendix N.1 failure cases show visible identity drift once >4-6% of steps are replaced), yet the paper does not provide a principled or automatic way to select the replacement fraction, relying instead on a fixed small percentage found empirically per model.

Presentation quality issues (e.g., duplicated reference entries [23]/[24] for the same paper, dense reliance on many small ad hoc metrics/tables rather than a few decisive controlled experiments) suggest the paper would benefit from tighter focus and more rigorous experimental design rather than breadth of loosely connected observations.

strengths: Very thorough empirical study across six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space ADMs at multiple resolutions, latent-space LDM/DiT, both conditional and unconditional), which strengthens the generality of the claims.

The paper poses a clear, well-motivated causal chain: (1) latents deviate from Gaussian noise, (2) this deviation is spatially concentrated in smooth/plain image regions, (3) it originates from higher approximation error during the earliest inversion steps, and (4) this has measurable downstream consequences for interpolation and editing diversity. Each step is backed by dedicated experiments (correlation statistics, triangle-angle geometry, variance analysis, per-step error decomposition).

The proposed fix (replacing only the first few percent of DDIM inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap (only ~4% extra compute), and shown to be effective at decorrelating latents while largely preserving reconstruction quality, which is a practically appealing takeaway for practitioners using inversion for editing/interpolation.

Extensive and honest appendix material: limitations section explicitly notes failure cases (e.g., CelebA-trained LDM, high-step-count degradation, large-percentage replacement hurting reconstruction), broader impact discussion, compute resource reporting, and additional studies on noise-to-image mapping and training dynamics that support and extend the main claims.

Quantitative evaluation uses multiple relevant metrics (FID/Precision/Recall for interpolation, DreamSim/LPIPS/SSIM/DINO/CLIP-T for editing diversity and alignment) rather than relying on a single proxy, and qualitative figures corroborate the quantitative trends.
weaknesses: The paper does not include direct quantitative comparisons against existing inversion-improvement methods designed to address similar editability/correlation issues (e.g., Renoise, edit-friendly DDPM inversion, null-text inversion, Parmar et al.'s regularization). All comparisons are against naive DDIM inversion and the noise baseline, making it hard to judge whether the proposed fix is competitive with or superior to prior remedies for the same problem.

The core diagnostic finding that DDIM-inverted latents deviate from Gaussian noise and are less editable is not entirely new (acknowledged citations to Parmar et al., Garibi et al., Huberman-Spiegelglas et al.); the paper's novelty rests mainly on the finer-grained spatial/temporal attribution (plain regions, early steps) and the specific fix, which is a comparatively incremental contribution.

The proposed solution is conceptually simple (essentially re-noising the image directly for the first few steps instead of inverting), and its trade-off against reconstruction fidelity is only explored qualitatively in the appendix (failure cases); a more systematic quantitative sweep of reconstruction-error vs. editability trade-off across the tested percentage range would strengthen the practical guidance.

As noted in the limitations, the approach and analysis appear less applicable to models trained on narrower, uniform-background datasets (e.g., CelebA-HQ LDM), and the generalization to more diverse/complex modern text-to-image backbones (e.g., large-scale Stable Diffusion/DiT variants beyond the tested IF/DiT) is not demonstrated.

The user-facing benefit of the method (better interpolation/editing diversity) is evaluated with automated metrics and a modest number of qualitative examples; a human study or larger-scale qualitative evaluation would make the claims about 'higher quality' edits more convincing, since metrics like FID/DreamSim only partially capture perceptual editing quality.

strengths: Thorough and systematic empirical analysis of DDIM inversion latents across six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space unconditional ADMs, conditional pixel models IF/DiT, and a latent diffusion model), providing good generality of the claimed phenomenon.

Careful causal tracing of the observed correlation/low-diversity phenomenon to the first few inversion steps and to reduced variance/higher error in noise predictions for smooth ('plain') image regions, supported by multiple complementary analyses (Pearson correlation tables, geometric triangle/angle analysis, per-step error decomposition, PNG compressibility).

The proposed fix (replacing the first few DDIM inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap, and shown empirically to decorrelate latents close to Gaussian noise levels while incurring minimal reconstruction cost, and is compared against several existing inversion-improvement baselines (Pix2Pix-Zero, ReNoise, DPMSolver) with favorable trade-offs.

Extensive appendix content that strengthens the main claims: robustness across different numbers of inversion steps (T=1000), analysis over the course of model training showing the noise-latent relationship stabilizes early, an interesting noise-to-image/latent mapping asymmetry study, and honest reporting of failure cases and limitations.

Practical downstream demonstrations (interpolation quality via FID/precision/recall, image editing diversity/text-alignment via DreamSim/LPIPS/CLIP) showing consistent, non-trivial improvements from the fix, plus a bonus qualitative demonstration of stochastic editing of real images enabled by the fix.
weaknesses: The core phenomenon (DDIM inversion latents deviating from Gaussian noise, correlations, reduced editability) has already been noted in prior works cited by the paper itself (Garibi et al. 2024, Parmar et al. 2023, Hong et al. 2024, Wallace et al. 2023); the main novelty here is a more detailed empirical characterization and localization to plain regions/first steps rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon or theory.

The proposed fix is conceptually very close to existing SDEdit-style partial renoising and is a fairly simple heuristic (replace first t' steps with forward diffusion); no principled/adaptive method is proposed for choosing t' beyond manual sweeps, and the appendix shows the fix can fail (significant content changes) once too many steps are replaced.

The paper does not include a comparison to some other recent inversion methods explicitly designed for exact/high-fidelity inversion (e.g., EDICT, exact DPM-Solver inversion of Hong et al. 2024 beyond the one baseline table, BELM) across the full suite of experiments (correlation, editing, interpolation), limiting the completeness of the baseline comparison.

Some quantitative results (e.g., Table 6, Figure 7) show relatively modest absolute differences between methods, and statistical significance/variance across seeds is not always discussed, making it hard to judge how robust some of the reported improvements are.

The theoretical explanation for why plain regions specifically induce lower-diversity, higher-error noise predictions remains largely empirical/correlational (grounded in cited works on curvature/singularity near t→0) rather than derived rigorously within this paper, so the causal mechanism explanation is somewhat borrowed rather than newly established.

The practical significance of the fix for high-stakes applications (e.g., large-scale text-to-image editing pipelines with classifier-free guidance) is not directly tested, since CFG is disabled in the main correlation experiments (Section G) to isolate inversion error, leaving open how much the phenomenon and fix matter under realistic guided generation settings.

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical analysis across six diverse diffusion models (pixel-space and latent-space, conditional and unconditional, various resolutions), which gives the central claims reasonably broad empirical support.

Clear diagnostic narrative: the paper isolates the divergence of DDIM-inverted latents from Gaussian noise, localizes it to smooth/plain image regions, and traces it to elevated approximation error and reduced prediction diversity specifically in the first few inversion steps (Figs. 3-4, Table 3).

The proposed fix (replacing the first few inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap, and shown to decorrelate latents while incurring only minor reconstruction cost, with quantitative gains in interpolation (Fig. 5), text-guided editing diversity/alignment (Fig. 7, Table 6), and comparisons against several existing inversion-improvement baselines (Pix2Pix-Zero, ReNoise, DPMSolver; Table 7).

Very thorough appendix with many robustness checks (varying step counts up to T=1000, training-dynamics analysis of noise-image-latent relationships, angle/triangle geometry analysis, noise-to-image mapping asymmetry, failure cases, qualitative interpolation/editing examples), which strengthens confidence in the reported phenomena.
Well-organized research-question structure and generally clear writing/visualizations that make the empirical story easy to follow.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core observation that DDIM-inverted latents deviate from Gaussian noise and exhibit spatial correlations is already noted in several cited prior works (Parmar et al. 2023; Garibi et al. 2024; Huberman-Spiegelglas et al. 2024; Wallace et al. 2023); this paper mainly adds a more detailed localization/attribution and a very simple engineering fix rather than a fundamentally new method or theoretical account.

The proposed 'fix' — substituting initial inversion steps with plain forward diffusion — is conceptually close to well-known noise-injection tricks used in diffusion-based editing (e.g., SDEdit-style partial renoising), and the paper does not clearly differentiate its contribution from this existing practice beyond framing it explicitly within the inversion pipeline.

The explanation for why errors concentrate in plain regions leans heavily on borrowed theoretical arguments from other works (1/t curvature blow-up, noise-schedule singularities) rather than an independently derived or rigorous theoretical justification, leaving the mechanism somewhat under-explained.

The method's generality is undercut by an acknowledged exception (LDM on CelebA-HQ shows much weaker effects) and by the explicit limitation that the fix does not address inversion error at low step counts, where it can even degrade reconstruction (Fig. 22).

Quantitative comparisons in the main paper are restricted to a fairly narrow set of baselines and models (e.g., Table 7 only uses SDXL; Table 4/Fig. 7 only DiT/IF), and some choices (plain-surface threshold τ=0.025, choice of 4% vs other percentages) are not accompanied by sensitivity analysis in the main text.

Overall the contribution reads as an incremental, if careful, empirical characterization plus a straightforward mitigation, which may not meet the bar of a clearly novel or high-impact contribution expected at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Thorough, well-structured empirical investigation of a real and previously under-explained phenomenon: DDIM-inverted latents deviate from Gaussian noise, especially in smooth/plain image regions.
Analysis spans six diverse diffusion architectures (pixel-space unconditional ADMs, LDM, DiT, IF) and both conditioned/unconditioned settings, lending good generality to the claims.

Clear causal chain established: correlation observation -> localization to plain image regions -> attribution to inaccurate/low-diversity noise predictions in the first inversion steps -> demonstrated downstream consequences (interpolation and editing quality).

The proposed fix (replacing early inversion steps with forward diffusion) is simple, cheap (faster than DDIM inversion), and shown to be effective at decorrelating latents while minimally harming reconstruction, with quantitative comparisons against several existing inversion improvements (Pix2Pix-Zero, ReNoise, DPMSolver) in Table 7.

Extensive and thoughtful appendix: additional metrics (KL divergence, triangle-angle geometry), robustness checks across step counts up to T=1000, training-dynamics study showing when noise-image-latent relations emerge, honest failure-case analysis, and qualitative results for stochastic real-image editing and interpolation.
Good writing, clear framing via explicit research questions, and reasonable practical significance for editing/interpolation pipelines built on DDIM inversion.
weaknesses: The proposed remedy is conceptually very simple (substitute a small percentage of inversion steps with forward-diffusion noise); the technical novelty of the 'fix' itself is limited, and the paper's main contribution is more the diagnostic analysis than a new method.

The fix necessarily trades off reconstruction fidelity for editability/diversity (as shown in the failure-case appendix), but the paper does not provide much theoretical guidance or an adaptive/principled way to choose the fraction of steps to replace beyond empirical tuning (2-4%).

Comparisons to state-of-the-art editing-oriented inversion techniques (e.g., Null-text inversion, EDICT, more recent rectified-flow inversion methods) are somewhat limited to a single SDXL experiment (Table 7); broader head-to-head evaluation on established editing benchmarks (e.g., PIE-Bench) would strengthen claims of practical significance.

Quantitative editing/interpolation evaluations rely mostly on distributional or embedding-based diversity/quality metrics (FID, DreamSim, CLIP-T) without human evaluation, which may not fully capture perceptual quality or semantic correctness of edits.
Some effects (e.g., CelebA-HQ LDM in Appendix A) do not generalize well, and the explanation given for this exception is speculative rather than empirically verified.

The paper is dense with many research questions, tables, and appendix sections; while thorough, this could be streamlined, and some appendix analyses (e.g., training-dynamics study) feel tangential to the core message and are not tightly integrated with the main narrative.
